text: Dinosaur footprints are [[fossil|fossils]] of behaviour. A single print shows the shape of a foot. A line of prints, called a trackway, shows how the animal walked, how fast it was going and whether it was alone or in a group.

Footprints can also show things bones cannot. They prove that dinosaurs walked with their legs under their bodies and carried their tails off the ground. Footprints are far more common than skeletons, and they record animals in the place where they were alive, not where they died.

st.prompt: A trackway shows the prints of 20 long-necked dinosaurs all walking in the same direction, side by side. What does that suggest?

options.t: They were travelling together as a herd
One dinosaur walked past 20 times
The prints were made millions of years apart

st.reveal: Parallel tracks, evenly spaced and pointing the same way, made in the same layer of mud, suggest a group moving together. Bones alone could never tell us that animals lived in herds.

Scientists studied the claimed "human" prints at the Paluxy River in Glen Rose. They turned out to be worn or mud-filled dinosaur tracks, and some were carvings. No human tracks have ever been found with dinosaur tracks.

sec.t:
In 1802, a farm boy named Pliny Moody was ploughing a field in Massachusetts when he turned up a stone slab with three-toed prints. People at the time thought they had been made by giant birds, perhaps Noah's raven from the story of the flood.

In the 1830s, the [[geologist|geologist]] Edward Hitchcock collected thousands of these tracks in the Connecticut River valley. He too thought they were bird tracks. He was not as wrong as it sounds. The prints were left by meat-eating dinosaurs, the group that later gave rise to [[@birds-dinosaurs|birds]]. That is why many dinosaur tracks look like a chicken's footprints, only much bigger.

Each footprint is a little like a [[@fingerprints|fingerprint]], with its own shape. Scientists look at the number of toes, the claws and the width of the foot. Three slim toes with sharp tips usually mean a meat-eater. Wide, round prints mean a long-necked plant-eater. Leg length can be worked out from foot size, and the gap between prints gives the [[@dino-speed|speed]].

Matching a print to a [[species|species]] is hard, though. Many dinosaurs had similar feet, and the same foot left different prints in soft or firm mud. That is why tracks usually get their own names, separate from the animals that made them. A print called Eubrontes, for example, describes a shape of footprint, not a particular dinosaur. Scientists who study tracks, called ichnologists, also look at how the mud squeezed up around a foot. That can show whether the animal was slipping, turning or pushing off hard.

India has its share of tracks. Near [[@rajasthan-forts|Jaisalmer]] in Rajasthan, scientists have found three-toed footprints about 200 million years old, from the early Jurassic, pressed into rock that was once a beach. Footprints have also been reported from Kutch in Gujarat, along with eggs and bones in other parts of [[@dinos-in-india|the country]].

At Cal Orck'o in Bolivia, a quarry wall the size of several football fields holds thousands of footprints. The rock was once flat lakeshore mud, later tilted almost upright, so the tracks now seem to climb a cliff. Near Broome, in Western Australia, [[sauropod|sauropod]] prints about 1.7 m long are among the biggest ever found, long enough for a child to lie down in.

text: Being a dinosaur hunter, or palaeontologist, means a mix of long walks in hot, dusty places, careful digging with tiny tools and years of work in labs and museums. Most of the time is spent looking, not digging. [[fossil|Fossil]] hunters walk slowly over rocky hillsides, scanning the ground for bits of bone that have weathered out of the rock.

When they find something, the real work begins. They clear the rock around it, map and photograph every piece, wrap the bones in plaster and carry them out, sometimes by helicopter. Then preparators spend months or years freeing the bones from rock in a lab. Only after that can scientists study the animal and, if it is new, give it a name.

st.prompt: How do palaeontologists protect a big dinosaur bone before moving it?

options.t: Wrap it in strips of cloth soaked in plaster, like a cast for a broken arm
Freeze it in a block of ice
Paint it with bright colours

st.reveal: Fossil bones are often cracked and fragile. Diggers cover them with paper or foil, then wrap them in burlap strips dipped in wet plaster. When the plaster hardens, the "jacket" holds everything together so it can be flipped, lifted and trucked to a lab.

sec.t:
Dinosaur fossils are found in sedimentary rocks, layers of mud and sand that built up while dinosaurs were alive, between about 230 and 66 million years ago. The best hunting grounds are badlands: dry, rocky places with little soil or plants, where wind and rain keep wearing away the rock and exposing new fossils.

Famous dinosaur country includes the Hell Creek area of Montana and the Dakotas, the Gobi Desert in Mongolia, Alberta in Canada and Patagonia in Argentina. In India, dinosaur fossils come from rocks along the Narmada valley in Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh, and from the Godavari valley.

In August 1990, a team was digging near Faith, South Dakota, when their truck got a flat tyre. While others drove to town for repairs, fossil hunter Sue Hendrickson walked to a cliff she had wanted to check. She spotted bones sticking out of the rock above her.

They belonged to a Tyrannosaurus rex, about 90% complete, one of the most complete ever found. It was named Sue after her. There was a long legal fight over who owned it. In 1997 the skeleton was sold for over 8 million dollars to the Field Museum in [[@chicago|Chicago]], where visitors still line up to see it.

India's fossil story began in the 1800s, when British officers found dinosaur bones near Jabalpur. In the early 1980s, [[geologist|geologists]] from the Geological Survey of India found bones of a large meat-eating dinosaur at Rahioli in Gujarat. Scientists from India and the US later studied them, and in 2003 named the animal [[@rajasaurus|Rajasaurus]], the "royal lizard".

Gujarat's Balasinor area has a dinosaur fossil park, and huge nesting grounds with fossil eggs have been found in Madhya Pradesh's Dhar district. Many Indian fossils come to light because farmers, road workers and schoolteachers notice something odd and report it.

Palaeontologists usually study geology or biology at university, then specialise. Many begin as children who collect rocks, visit museums and read all they can about the [[@dinos-in-india|dinosaurs of India]] or wherever they grew up. Some of the most important early finds were made by amateurs, like [[@mary-anning|Mary Anning]] in England in the 1800s.

Fossils are protected by law in many places, so never dig on your own. Joining a museum programme or a guided fossil trip is the safe way to start, and you might just spot the next great find.

text: When something unwanted gets inside an oyster's shell and can't be pushed out, the oyster covers it up. Special tissue called the mantle, the same tissue that builds the shell, wraps the intruder in a pouch. Then it coats it with thin layers of nacre, a hard, shiny material made of a [[mineral|mineral]] called calcium carbonate held together with [[protein|protein]].

Layer after layer builds up, thousands of them, each far thinner than a human hair. Over months and years, the lump grows into a smooth, gleaming pearl. Oysters are the best known, but freshwater mussels and some other shellfish can make pearls too.

A grain of sand

st.reveal: Sand gets into oysters all the time and is usually flushed out. Most natural pearls start with a tiny intruder, such as a parasite, or with a bit of the oyster's own shell-making tissue that ends up in the wrong place. The oyster walls it off with layer after layer of nacre.

sec.t:
A pearl's glow, called lustre, comes from its layers. Light passes into the outer layers, bounces off the ones beneath, and comes back out. The reflections overlap and create soft rainbow colours, the same shimmer you see inside many seashells.

That is also why pearls need care. Nacre is close to the mineral in chalk, so [[acid|acids]] such as vinegar or lemon juice can dull it, and hard grit can scratch it. A real pearl rubbed gently against the front teeth often feels slightly gritty, while a plastic copy feels smooth.

sec.h: How people learned to grow pearls
sec.t:
Natural pearls are rare. Divers might open hundreds of oysters to find one good pearl. In the 1890s, a Japanese noodle-seller's son named Kokichi Mikimoto began farming oysters and placing small beads inside them by hand. His first success, in 1893, was a half-round pearl. Over the next few decades, Japanese researchers worked out how to grow fully round pearls.

Today, a pearl farmer slips a polished bead and a tiny square of mantle tissue from another oyster inside each shell. The oyster coats the bead with nacre, just as it would an intruder. After one to three years or more, the pearl is harvested. Almost all pearls sold today are cultured like this, mostly from China, Japan, Indonesia, Australia and French Polynesia.

Pearls are not all white. Depending on the kind of oyster and the water it lives in, they can be cream, gold, pink, silver, grey or nearly black. The large dark pearls of Tahiti come from black-lipped oysters.

Unlike [[@gems-crystals|gems]] such as diamonds, which are dug out of rock and cut into shape, a pearl comes out of the shell ready to wear. People in [[@japan-culture|Japan]], India and many other places have treasured that natural finish for centuries. Diving for pearls was once a way of life from the Persian Gulf to the coasts of Australia. In Bahrain, an old pearling trail through the town of Muharraq is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

text: Yes, pirates were real, and they still exist. A pirate is someone who attacks and robs ships at sea. Piracy is as old as sailing itself. Ancient Egyptians, Greeks and Romans all complained about sea raiders, and in 75 BCE pirates even kidnapped a young Julius Caesar and held him for ransom.

The pirates most people picture lived during the "Golden Age of Piracy", from about 1650 to 1730. They attacked treasure ships and merchant ships in the Caribbean, along the coast of North America and in the Indian Ocean. Some, like Blackbeard, became famous in their own lifetimes.

st.reveal: Robert Louis Stevenson's Treasure Island, published in 1883, made treasure maps, one-legged cooks and talking parrots famous. Real pirates usually spent or shared their loot quickly. Very few are known to have buried any.

sec.t:
Many pirates were former sailors who had escaped harsh treatment on navy or merchant ships. A pirate ship could be crowded, dirty and dangerous, but it offered a share of the loot and some say in how things were run.

Many crews signed written rules, called articles. They set out how prizes would be shared, how much money an injured pirate would get, and how quarrels would be settled. Crews often elected their captain by vote and could remove him. Pirates were still violent criminals who stole, threatened and sometimes killed. Most were caught or died young.

Edward Teach, better known as Blackbeard, was one of the most feared pirates of all. He is said to have tied slow-burning fuses into his long black beard to look terrifying in battle. In 1718 he blockaded the harbour of Charleston, South Carolina, for about a week.

Later that year, he was killed in a fight with British navy sailors off the coast of North Carolina. In 1996, divers found a wreck near Beaufort, North Carolina, now identified as his flagship, Queen Anne's Revenge. [[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] have since raised cannons, anchors and thousands of smaller objects, turning the [[@shipwrecks|shipwreck]] into a window on real pirate life.

One of the richest pirate raids of the age happened near India. In 1695, the English pirate Henry Every attacked the Ganj-i-Sawai, a huge ship belonging to the [[@mughals|Mughal]] emperor Aurangzeb, as it sailed home from the Red Sea with pilgrims and treasure.

The emperor was furious and blamed the English. For a time, the [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] feared it might lose its right to trade in India, and it had to promise to help guard Mughal ships. Every himself disappeared, and nobody knows for sure what became of him.

Who counts as a pirate can depend on who is telling the story. [[@kanhoji-angre|Kanhoji Angre]], admiral of the [[@marathas|Maratha]] navy in the early 1700s, attacked British and Portuguese ships along the west coast. The British called him a pirate. Many in India remember him as a naval commander defending his coast.

{{story:east-india-company}}

In 1883, Robert Louis Stevenson published Treasure Island. Its buried treasure, maps marked with an X, wooden legs and parrots shaped how pirates have been shown ever since. The black flag with a skull and crossbones was real, though. Different pirates flew different versions to frighten ships into giving up without a fight.

Piracy has not ended. In the 2000s, pirates from Somalia attacked ships in the Gulf of Aden and the Arabian Sea. Navies from many countries, including India and the United States, now patrol these waters to protect sailors.

text: India has several kinds of deer, from tiny, barking forest deer to big, shaggy stags that weigh more than a motorbike. The most common is the chital, or spotted deer, often seen in herds in national parks. The biggest is the sambar. Others include the barasingha, or swamp deer, the hog deer, the barking deer, the sangai of Manipur and the hangul of Kashmir.

All male deer grow [[antler|antlers]], branching bony crowns that fall off every year and grow back bigger. India also has musk deer and mouse deer, which look like deer and are close cousins but belong to separate families. Many of India's deer are prey for tigers and leopards, so they live on high alert.

st.reveal: Deer antlers are made of bone and grow fast each year, covered at first in soft, furry skin called velvet. After the breeding season, they drop off and new ones begin to grow. Horns, like a blackbuck's, have a bony core covered in keratin and are never shed.

sec.t:
The sambar is India's largest deer. A big stag can weigh more than 250 kilograms and stand about as tall at the shoulder as a grown-up. It lives in thick forest, comes out mostly at night and loves wallowing in water. When frightened, it stamps a foot and gives a loud, honking bell.

The Indian muntjac, or barking deer, is small, about the size of a large dog. Its alarm call sounds like a dog's bark and can carry a long way through the forest at dusk. Males have short antlers and two small tusks that poke down from the upper jaw.

The barasingha, or swamp deer, is named for its antlers. "Bara singha" means twelve tines, and a big stag can have twelve or more points. A hard-ground kind of barasingha lives only in central India. By 1970, only about 66 remained, all in [[@madhya-pradesh|Kanha]] in Madhya Pradesh.

Forest staff protected their meadows, relocated some villages with compensation, and fenced off breeding areas. The herd recovered, and recent counts have found more than 1,000 in Kanha, with some moved to other reserves to start new herds.

sec.h: Deer of the valleys and lakes
sec.t:
The hangul, also called the Kashmir stag, is a kind of red deer found mainly in Dachigam National Park near Srinagar, in [[@kashmir|Kashmir]]. It is the official animal of Jammu and Kashmir. Its numbers fell to a few hundred, and a 2025 [[census|census]] counted 323, up from 289 in 2023.

The sangai, a kind of Eld's deer, lives only around Keibul Lamjao National Park, on [[@india-wonder-loktak|Loktak Lake]] in [[@northeast-india|Manipur]]. The park is the world's only floating national park, made of thick mats of floating plants called phumdis. The deer walk delicately across these soft islands, which may be why they are called dancing deer. The sangai is Manipur's state animal, and only a few hundred survive.

Antlers are among the fastest-growing bone tissue of any animal. While growing, they are covered in soft, furry skin called velvet, full of blood vessels. When fully grown, the velvet dries and the stag rubs it off on trees, leaving hard, bare bone for fighting rivals in the breeding season.

Afterwards the antlers drop off, and a new set starts. This is a quick way to tell deer from antelopes like the blackbuck and nilgai, whose horns stay on for life. Spotted coats, sharp ears and lightning-fast reflexes all help deer stay alive in forests full of [[predator|predators]]. Even a [[@tiger-stripes|tiger's stripes]] are designed to fool a deer's eyes.

text: Donkeys can carry heavy loads over rough, dry ground, on little food and water, for hours. They are calm, sure-footed and tough. For thousands of years, that made them the most practical helpers a poor farmer, trader or potter could own.

Their wild ancestor, the African wild ass, lived in the deserts and stony hills of north-eastern Africa. Animals from such harsh places learn to cope with heat, thirst and thin grass. Donkeys kept those talents when people tamed them, which is why they still work in deserts and mountains across Asia, Africa and Latin America.

myth: Donkeys are stupid and stubborn.
Donkeys are cautious. When a horse is scared it tends to run, but a donkey often stops and thinks about the danger first. People who work with them say they learn well and remember routes for years.

sec.t:
A big study of donkey DNA, published in 2022, found that donkeys were [[domesticate|domesticated]] about 7,000 years ago in eastern Africa, around today's Kenya and the Horn of Africa. Early herders may have used them as the deserts there grew drier.

From Africa, donkeys spread to Egypt, West Asia and beyond. They carried goods on early trade routes long before [[@camels|camels]] were tamed. A donkey [[caravan|caravan]] could cross country with no roads, stopping each night at wells it knew. Egyptian pharaohs had donkeys buried near their tombs. In the Bible, the Quran and Hindu stories, donkeys appear as ordinary working animals, carrying people, water and grain.

A donkey's hooves are small, hard and upright, good for stony slopes. Its big ears help it hear other donkeys across wide, empty land, and give off heat on hot days. Its loud bray carries a long way, useful when herds spread out to find food.

Donkeys also get much of the water they need from dry plants and can drink a lot quickly when they find it. Instead of running from danger as horses do, a donkey often freezes, studies the problem, and may stand its ground or kick. People called that stubbornness. On a narrow mountain path, it can save a life.

Donkeys still carry bricks at [[kiln|kilns]], sand from riverbeds and goods up hill paths. But as trucks and tractors spread, their numbers have fallen fast. India's 2019 livestock [[census|census]] counted about 1.2 lakh donkeys, less than half the number in 2012. Some breeds, such as the Halari donkey of Gujarat, are now rare. Its milk is sold for soap and skin creams, which has given some herders a new reason to keep them.

India also has a wild relative. The Indian wild ass, or *khur*, lives on the salt flats of the [[@gujarat-rann|Rann of Kutch]] in Gujarat. It can run at about 50 km/h. In the 1960s only a few hundred were left. A 2024 count found 7,672, thanks to strict protection of its home.

text: When marching army ants reach a gap, such as a space between two leaves or a dip in a branch, one ant stops at the edge and stretches across. Another walks onto it and grips on, then another. Each ant hooks its claws onto its neighbours' legs and bodies. Within seconds, there is a living bridge, and the rest of the column streams across.

No ant is in charge. Each one follows simple rules. If it feels other ants walking over it, it holds still. If the traffic stops, it lets go and rejoins the march. When the column has passed, the bridge melts away, ant by ant, as each one climbs off and follows the others.

st.prompt: Who tells the army ants where to build a bridge?

options.t: Nobody. Each ant follows simple rules about where it feels traffic
The queen sends orders with smells
Older "engineer" ants direct the others

st.reveal: There is no leader or plan. An ant that reaches a gap and gets walked over stays still. If traffic over it stops, it lets go and walks off. Thousands of these tiny decisions add up to a bridge in exactly the right place.

sec.h: A bridge that thinks for itself
sec.t:
In 2015, scientists in Panama tested army ants on a track with a V-shaped gap. The ants built a bridge near the point of the V, where the gap was small. Then, over several minutes, the bridge slowly moved down the V, towards the open end, making the route shorter.

But it stopped partway. Building further out would have needed too many ants in the bridge, and those ants could not carry food. The bridge settled where shortcuts and lost workers balanced out. No ant can see the whole bridge, and most army ants can barely see at all. Yet together they solved a trade-off that engineers would need a calculator for.

Army ants are not the only builders. When their nests flood, fire ants link their legs and float as a raft. The ants' waxy, hairy bodies trap air bubbles, so a raft of thousands can drift on water for days.

Weaver ants, which live in India, Southeast Asia and Australia, form chains to pull two leaves together. One ant grabs the edge of a leaf, another grabs its waist, and so on, until the chain can tug the leaf into place. Then other workers hold their [[larva|larvae]] like glue sticks, which ooze silk to stitch the leaves into a nest. In parts of Odisha, people cook these red ants and their eggs into a sharp, sour chutney called *kai chutney*.

Engineers study ant bridges for ideas. Swarms of small robots that join up to cross gaps or climb walls could help in disasters, reaching places too dangerous for people. Each [[@robots|robot]] would follow simple rules, like an ant, instead of waiting for orders from a central computer.

The same idea, many simple parts making one clever whole, turns up in bird flocks and fish schools. It also turns up in the way humans build things. Engineers have spent centuries learning to make [[@bridges|bridges]] stay up with steel and concrete. Army ants do it with their own bodies, and then walk away, leaving no trace.

sec.t:
अब तक मिली सबसे पुरानी लिखी धुन आज के सीरिया के प्राचीन शहर उगारित से आती है। इसे लगभग 3,400 साल पहले [[@mesopotamia|मेसोपोटामिया]] की कील जैसी लिपि में मिट्टी की पट्टियों पर दबाकर लिखा गया था। विद्वान आज भी बहस करते हैं कि यह ठीक-ठीक कैसी सुनाई देती होगी।

प्राचीन यूनानी शब्दों के ऊपर अक्षर लिखकर संगीत लिखते थे। लगभग 2,000 साल पहले एक समाधि के पत्थर पर उकेरा गया एक छोटा यूनानी गीत अपने सुरों समेत पूरा बचा है। उसके बोल सुनने वाले से कहते हैं कि जब तक ज़िंदगी है, उसका आनंद लो।

हाथ से संगीत की नकल करना धीमा काम था और उसमें गलतियाँ भरी रहती थीं। 1501 में [[@venice|वेनिस]] में ओत्तावियानो पेत्रुच्ची नाम के एक छापेखाने वाले ने चलायमान टाइप से गीतों की एक किताब छापी। यह यूरोप में [[@printing-press|छापाखाना]] आने के लगभग पचास साल बाद हुआ।

छपे हुए संगीत से संगीतकार अपना काम दूर-दूर तक पहुँचा सके। विएना में लिखी कोई रचना कुछ ही महीनों बाद लंदन में बजाई जा सकती थी। छपी स्वरलिपियाँ बड़ा कारोबार बन गईं, और 1800 के दशक तक यूरोप और अमेरिका के बहुत-से मध्यमवर्गीय घरों में एक पियानो और छपे गीतों का एक ढेर होता था।

भारतीय संगीत में सुरों का विचार बहुत पुराना है। *सामवेद* के वैदिक मंत्र सुर के तय उतार-चढ़ाव के साथ गाए जाते थे। पर शास्त्रीय संगीत ज़्यादातर लिखे पन्नों के बजाय गुरु-शिष्य के रिश्ते पर टिका रहा।

1900 की शुरुआत में संगीतशास्त्री विष्णु नारायण भातखंडे ने पूरे भारत में घूमकर बंदिशें जमा कीं और हिंदुस्तानी संगीत के लिए एक स्वरलिपि पद्धति बनाई। कर्नाटक संगीत ने भी लिखने के अपने ढंग विकसित किए। फिर भी, जैसा [[@carnatic-hindustani|कर्नाटक और हिंदुस्तानी संगीत]] में समझाया गया है, ज़्यादातर संगीतकार कहते हैं कि कागज़ बस याद दिलाने के लिए है। असली संगीत सुनने में बसता है।

स्टाफ़ पर सुरों के आकार बताते हैं कि हर आवाज़ कितनी देर रोकनी है। खोखला अंडाकार देर तक चलता है। उसे भर दो और एक डंडी लगा दो, तो वह आधी देर या उससे भी कम चलता है। झंडियाँ और जोड़ने वाली पट्टियाँ सुरों को और छोटा कर देती हैं।

शुरुआत में लिखे अंक, जिन्हें टाइम सिग्नेचर कहते हैं, बताते हैं कि हर हिस्से (बार) में कितनी मात्राएँ हैं, कुछ-कुछ वैसे ही जैसे हमारे तीनताल में 16 मात्राएँ होती हैं। बड़ा [[@orchestra|ऑर्केस्ट्रा]] इन्हीं सब पर टिका है, ताकि अलग-अलग पन्ने पढ़ते सौ संगीतकार भी एक ही ताल पर पहुँचें। तालों के बारे में और जानने के लिए [[@rhythm-beat|ताल]] पढ़ो।

text: Medicine is about treating one sick person. Public health is about keeping whole populations from getting sick in the first place. It includes clean drinking water, [[@toilets-sewers|sewers]], [[vaccine|vaccines]], food safety checks, [[@mosquitoes-bite|mosquito control]], clean air, [[@road-safety|road safety]] and advice on healthy eating.

Most public health work is invisible when it succeeds. You don't notice the [[@disease-history|cholera]] that never arrived or the measles outbreak that didn't happen. Yet these efforts have saved more lives than almost anything else people have done. In India, life expectancy was around 32 years at independence in 1947. Today it is about 70.

Medicine matters, but much of the gain came from public health work, such as clean water, sewers, vaccines, better food and safer homes. These protect millions of people before they ever need a doctor.

sec.t:
Smallpox killed hundreds of millions of people over the centuries. From 1967, the World Health Organization led a huge campaign to find every case and vaccinate everyone around it. India was a major battleground, and health workers searched village by village, house by house. India's last case was in 1975. In 1980, WHO declared [[@smallpox|smallpox]] gone from the whole planet, the first human disease ever wiped out.

Polio came next. India's Pulse Polio campaign, begun in 1995, sent vaccinators to give drops to every child under five, on set days, wherever they were. India's last case of wild polio was a girl in Howrah, West Bengal, in January 2011.

Most public health is less dramatic. Inspectors check that milk is safe. Teams spray to control the [[@what-if-no-mosquitoes|mosquitoes]] that carry [[@mosquito-diseases|malaria and dengue]]. Iodine added to salt has helped prevent goitre, a swelling in the neck. Laws on [[@seatbelts|seat belts]], smoking and clean air are public health too.

Cities learned many of these lessons the hard way. When [[@black-death|plague]] reached Bombay in 1896, it killed many thousands of people over the following years. In response, the city set up an Improvement Trust in 1898 to clear crowded, airless lanes and build better housing. Clean water and drains changed city life more than almost any medicine.

In the USA, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention began in 1946 with fighting malaria in the southern states. Today it tracks outbreaks and studies everything from food poisoning to road injuries.

Public health depends on trust and cooperation. A vaccine only stops an outbreak if enough people take it. During the COVID-19 [[pandemic|pandemic]], people around the world wore masks, kept apart and got vaccinated. Those choices showed how one person's health is tied to everyone else's.

Since 1948, the World Health Organization has helped countries share information and respond to outbreaks. Its founding day, 7 April, is now celebrated as World Health Day. Some of the biggest health victories of the next century may come from something as simple as a clean tap.

text: The Sustainable Development Goals, often called the Global Goals, are a list of 17 aims that all 193 member countries of the [[@united-nations|United Nations]] agreed on in September 2015. Together they describe the kind of world countries promised to build by 2030.

The first goal is to end poverty everywhere. Others include [[@hunger|zero hunger]], good health, quality education, equal rights for girls and women, clean water and toilets, clean energy, and action on [[@climate-change|climate change]]. The last goal is about countries working together, because none of the others can be met by one country alone.
"[[sustainable|Sustainable]]" means meeting people's needs today without wrecking the chances of people who come later.

sec.t:
Each big goal is split into smaller targets, 169 in all. Goal 4, quality education, includes a target that all girls and boys finish primary and secondary school. Goal 6 includes clean drinking water for everyone.

Each target also has numbers that can be measured, such as how many children are in school or how many homes have a toilet. Every year the UN publishes a report on how the world is doing. That turns a list of hopes into something closer to a school report card.

The goals are not laws. No country is punished for missing them. They work more like a promise made in public, which governments, charities and companies can be held to.

Many targets are linked. Clean water cuts disease, healthier children miss fewer school days, and children who finish school tend to earn more as adults. Progress on one goal often helps several others, and failure on one can drag the rest down.

{{story:climate-change}}

They replaced an earlier list, the Millennium Development Goals, which ran from 2000 to 2015. That list had 8 goals and focused mainly on poorer countries. Some of it went well. The share of the world's people living in extreme poverty fell sharply during those years.

For the new list, the UN held talks and [[@surveys|surveys]] that asked millions of people around the world what mattered to them. The result was longer and broader. This time, rich countries like the USA had goals to meet too, on things like waste, fair pay and pollution.

The goals even got their own look: 17 bright coloured squares, each with a simple icon, which you may have spotted on school walls.

India's planning body, NITI Aayog, began ranking states on the goals in 2018 with its SDG India Index. Each state gets a score out of 100 for things like health, schooling, clean energy and hunger. Kerala has often come out near the top.

Some Indian programmes connect directly to the goals. The free [[@mid-day-meal|mid-day meal]] in government schools helps with hunger, health and education all at once. A child who eats lunch at school is more likely to keep coming to class.

By 2024 the deadline was getting close. The UN's report that year found that only about 17% of the targets were on track. The COVID-19 [[pandemic|pandemic]], wars and rising food prices had pushed many countries backwards.

That does not make the goals useless. Targets give people something to measure, argue about and push for. A village that gets [[@water-purify|clean drinking water]], or a girl who stays in school for two more years, counts toward the list whether or not the whole world finishes on time.

text: You count a billion people the slow way: one home at a time. In a census, the government trains an army of counters, called enumerators. Each one is given a small patch of streets or villages, and visits every household in it. They ask the same questions everywhere: who lives here, how old they are, what work they do.

All the counting is tied to one exact moment. India's 2011 census counted people as they were at midnight on 1 March 2011. Babies born after that moment were left out, so the totals don't keep shifting while the counting goes on. Then millions of forms are added up, and a country finds out how many of its people there are, and where.

sec.t:
A census really happens in two steps. First, counters walk every lane to list every building and home, so nothing gets missed later. Months afterwards, they return to count the people inside.

In India in 2011, about 27 lakh enumerators and supervisors did the work, many of them schoolteachers. They reached high mountain villages, island homes and [[@slums-housing|city slums]] alike. Special teams counted homeless people on a chosen night, at railway platforms and under flyovers.

The result: about 121 crore people, roughly a sixth of the world's [[@population|population]]. India's next census, delayed by the COVID-19 [[pandemic|pandemic]], began with house listing in April 2026 and is due to count people in February 2027. It is the first to collect answers mainly on mobile phones rather than paper.

sec.h: The machine that sped it up

sec.t:
A census decides real things. In the USA, the totals set how many seats each state gets in the House of Representatives, part of [[@congress-usa|Congress]]. In India, census numbers help plan where to build schools, hospitals and roads, and how to share money between states.

The questions also show how a country changes. Censuses record how many people can read, which languages they speak at home, and how many have [[@migration-india|moved from villages to cities]]. A huge pile of [[@big-numbers|big numbers]] slowly turns into a picture of everyday life.

Every census misses some people and counts a few twice. Families move. Some people are away, or worried about strangers asking questions. In the USA, studies after recent censuses found that young children were among the people most often missed.

To catch errors, statisticians run a second, smaller survey soon after the main count. They visit a sample of areas again and compare the two lists. The gap tells them roughly how many people slipped through. A census is less like a perfect photograph and more like a very careful sketch, checked twice.

text: Football is the world's most popular sport because almost anyone can play it, almost anywhere. You need a ball, or something like one, and two things to mark a goal. The basic rule, get the ball in the net without using your hands, is something a four-year-old understands.

It also spread early. British sailors, soldiers, traders and teachers carried it around the world in the 19th century, and local people made it their own. Today FIFA, the world body, has 211 member associations, more than the [[@united-nations|United Nations]] has member countries.

sec.h: Cheap to play, easy to start
sec.t:
Cricket needs bats, pads and a pitch. Hockey needs sticks. [[@basketball|Basketball]] needs a hoop. Football needs only a ball, and children in many countries make their own from rags, plastic bags or rolled-up socks. Some of the world's greatest players learned on dusty streets, not grass.

A game can have three players a side or eleven. It works on a beach, in a school corridor or on a muddy field in the rain. Nobody has to buy anything before they can join in.

A football match often ends 1–0, or even 0–0. That sounds dull, but it makes every goal precious. Fans can hold their breath for 90 minutes waiting for one moment. A weaker team can defend all match, score once and beat a famous one, which happens far more often than in sports with high scores.

That tension is a large part of the appeal. Each match is a story that nobody knows the ending of.

Football reached India with the British, and Bengal took to it fiercely. In 1911 Mohun Bagan, a club from Calcutta, beat a British army team to win the IFA Shield. Most of the Indian players played barefoot. Coming at a time of anger against British rule, the win was celebrated as a national triumph.

The rivalry between Mohun Bagan and East Bengal still fills stadiums in [[@kolkata|Kolkata]]. India won the football gold at the Asian Games in 1951 and 1962 and finished fourth at the 1956 Olympics.

sec.h: A game the whole world watches
sec.t:
The men's World Cup is the most watched sporting event on Earth. FIFA says about 1.5 billion people watched the 2022 final in Qatar. In 2026 the [[tournament|tournament]] was shared by the USA, Canada and Mexico and grew to 48 teams for the first time.

In the United States, the women's national team has won four Women's World Cups and made football one of the most popular sports for American girls. Scientists study how players [[@sport-science-football-curve|bend a free kick around a wall]], using the same physics that makes a [[@baseball-curve|baseball curve]]. Clubs now hire [[@sports-science|sports scientists]] to track every sprint. Yet the game a child plays with a paper ball in a lane is, in every way that matters, the same game.

text: Hollywood is a district of [[@los-angeles|Los Angeles]], in southern California. In the early 1900s, America's film companies were mostly based in [[@new-york|New York]] and New Jersey. Over about ten years, many moved across the country to Hollywood and the towns around it.

They came for three main reasons. Southern California had sunshine nearly every day, which early [[@cameras-how|cameras]] badly needed. Land was cheap, so studios could build huge outdoor sets. And within a day's drive there were beaches, deserts, mountains and forests, so one place could look like many. By the 1920s, "Hollywood" had become a name for the whole American film industry.

st.prompt: In the 1910s, why did filmmakers care so much about sunny weather?

options.t: Early film needed lots of bright light, and electric lamps were weak
Actors refused to work in the cold
Rain damaged the paper the films were printed on

st.reveal: Early film was not very sensitive to light, so scenes were often shot outdoors or on stages with glass or open roofs. Southern California has sunshine on most days of the year, which meant filming could go on almost all year round.

src: Britannica, Hollywood.

src.Library of Congress, Inventing Entertain: The Motion Pictures of the Edison Companies.

src: Hollywood Sign Trust, history of the sign.
n.certNote: Sunshine, cheap land and varied scenery are agreed reasons for the move west. How much filmmakers were also running away from Thomas Edison's patent lawyers is still argued over by historians.

d.try: Use a torch and a toy or doll in a dark room to test lighting like an early film crew. Light the toy from above, from the side and from below. Notice how each one changes the toy's mood. Filmmakers still use these same tricks.
myth: Most Hollywood films are still made in Hollywood.

Today many "Hollywood" films are shot in places such as Georgia, Canada, the UK and New Zealand, where costs are lower or the scenery fits. The word now means the American film business as a whole, not just one neighbourhood.
facts: a district of Los Angeles, California

sec.t:
Thomas Edison's company held many of the key patents for making and showing films. In 1908 Edison and other big companies formed the Motion Picture Patents Company. It demanded fees from anyone using their kind of camera or film, and took rule-breakers to court.

Some independent filmmakers found California handy because it was far from New Jersey, where Edison was based. Historians still argue about how much this mattered. The weather and the land were probably the bigger reasons, but escaping the patent fights helped.

By the 1920s a few giant studios ran Hollywood, among them Paramount, MGM, Warner Bros. and Universal. Each worked like a factory. Writers, actors, set builders and camera crews were on long contracts, and a big studio could finish a film every week or two.

In 1927 Warner Bros. released *The Jazz Singer*, the first feature film with synchronised talking scenes. Silent stars who had strange voices or strong accents sometimes lost their careers almost overnight. Two years later, in 1929, the first Academy Awards were handed out at a dinner that lasted about 15 minutes.

In 1923, property developers put up giant letters on a hillside reading HOLLYWOODLAND to advertise new homes. Each letter was about 15 metres tall, roughly as high as a five-storey building, and was lit with thousands of bulbs.

The sign fell into ruin over the years. In 1949 the last four letters were removed, leaving HOLLYWOOD. In 1978 the old wooden letters were replaced with steel ones paid for by donors, each sponsoring one letter.

Studios still have offices in and around Hollywood, but filming happens all over the world. Computers now create cities, storms and creatures that would once have needed huge sets, as [[@special-effects|special effects]] explains. Streaming services also make films without ever showing them in cinemas.

India's film industries, led by [[@bollywood|Bollywood]] and the southern film industries, make more films each year than Hollywood does. Hollywood films, though, still earn the most money worldwide, and those white letters on the hill still mean "the movies" to people almost everywhere.

text: Ludo comes from pachisi, a board game played in India for hundreds of years. Pachisi uses a cross-shaped board, often sewn from cloth, with four arms of squares and a home in the middle. Each player races four pieces around the board and back home, knocking rivals back to the start.

In the 1800s British people in India took the game home. In 1896 a simpler version was patented in England as ludo, Latin for "I play". It had a printed board, coloured counters and a cube-shaped die. The same game also crossed to America as Parcheesi. Today ludo is played on phones by millions of people, many of whom have never seen a cloth board.

st.prompt: In the old Indian game of pachisi, what did players usually throw to decide their moves?

options.t: Cowrie shells
Six-sided wooden dice
Coloured sticks with numbers painted on them

st.reveal: Players threw six or seven small cowrie shells and counted how many landed with the open side up. That number set the move. Some throws were worth more, with 25 the highest, which gave the game its name.

src: British Museum, games collections and notes on pachisi.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Pachisi and Ludo.
n.certNote: Pachisi is clearly the ancestor of ludo, and it is centuries old. Exactly when and where pachisi itself began is not known, and some popular stories about it are legends.

d.try: Play ludo with a twist. Instead of a die, throw five coins and count the heads, giving 0 to 5 moves. Play a game this way, then a game with a normal die. Talk about which felt fairer and why some numbers came up more often with the coins.
myth: Ludo was invented in England.
An English version was patented in 1896, but it was based on pachisi, which Indians had played for centuries. The English game simplified the board and used a cube die.
facts: pachisi, a cross-shaped board game from India
25, from the top throw of the shells
Parcheesi, sold in the USA since the 1800s

sec.t:
In traditional pachisi, players throw six or seven cowrie shells. Each shell can land with its open slit facing up or down. You count the open ones to get your move, and certain throws give bonus turns. The best throw was 25, or pachisi.

Shells make some numbers more likely than others, which you can work out with [[@probability|probability]]. A cube die is simpler, because each number from one to six has the same chance. That may be one reason the English version switched.

A related game, chaupar, uses long dice. A famous dice game in the Mahabharata, where the Pandavas lose their kingdom, is often linked to games like this.

{{story:probability}}

At Fatehpur Sikri, the city Emperor [[@akbar|Akbar]] built near Agra in the late 1500s, a courtyard floor is laid out like a giant pachisi board. A popular story says Akbar sat in the middle and played using real people as pieces, dressed in the right colours. There is no firm record that he did, and some historians think the pattern may be decoration. It remains one of the most repeated stories about the game.

What is clear is that pachisi was played across India by royalty and ordinary families alike, on embroidered cloth, on boards scratched into stone or simply drawn in the dust. It was often played in teams of two, with partners sitting opposite each other, and a cloth board could be rolled up with its cone-shaped wooden pieces and carried anywhere.

Once it reached Britain, ludo became a standard family game. Versions spread around the world under new names. Germany has Mensch ärgere Dich nicht, "Man, don't get annoyed". Spain has parchís. Like [[@snakes-ladders|snakes and ladders]], another game with Indian roots, it is often among the first [[@board-games|board games]] a child learns.

The rules change a little from home to home. In most versions you need a six to bring a piece out of its starting yard, and a six gives you another turn. Squares marked with a star are often safe, so nobody can capture you there. In the USA, Parcheesi was sold as "The Royal Game of India", and a later English game called Sorry! uses cards instead of dice for the same race-and-capture idea.

In 2016 a small Indian company launched an app called Ludo King. It grew slowly until 2020, when COVID-19 lockdowns kept families apart. Suddenly grandparents, cousins and friends were playing ludo together through their phones, from Delhi to Dallas.

The app became one of the most downloaded games in India. A game that left India on cloth boards and came back on screens had, in a way, returned home. The rules are much the same, and so is the groan when someone's piece gets sent back to the start just before reaching home.

text: There is no single strangest museum, because people find different things strange. But some real museums are very hard to beat. New Delhi has a museum about toilets. Near Boston, a museum displays art that is too bad to ignore. In Zagreb, in Croatia, a museum shows objects people kept from friendships and romances that ended.

What joins these odd places is a simple idea: almost anything can tell a story about people. A museum is a place that collects objects, looks after them and explains them, and some curators choose to do that with things nobody else bothers to keep.

st.prompt: James Smithson left his fortune to the United States to start the Smithsonian. How many times had he visited America?

options.t: Never
Once, as a young man
Every summer

st.reveal: Smithson was an English chemist who never set foot in the USA. His will left money to found an institution "for the increase and diffusion of knowledge". Nobody is quite sure why he chose America.

src: Smithsonian Institution, James Smithson and the founding of the Smithsonian.
Indian Museum, Kolkata, Ministry of Culture, Government of India.
Sulabh International, Sulabh International Museum of Toilets.
n.certNote: Which museum is "strangest" is a matter of opinion. The museums described here are real, and the facts about them are well documented.

d.try: Start a tiny museum on a shelf at home. Pick a theme, such as bottle caps, leaves or old bus tickets. Give each object a label card with what it is, where you found it and the date. Invite your family for an opening day and give them a short tour.
myth: Museums only keep old, precious treasures like gold crowns and famous paintings.
Many museums collect everyday things, from toilets and toys to bus tickets and bad art. Ordinary objects often tell us more about how people lived than treasures do.

sec.t:
The Museum of Bad Art began in 1994 near Boston, Massachusetts, when an antiques dealer found a painting sticking out of a rubbish pile. It showed an old woman dancing in a field, and it was memorably awful. Friends began collecting more.

The museum only takes works made in good faith, by people who were really trying. A painting must be bad in an interesting way, not merely dull. Visitors laugh, but many also leave thinking about what makes art good in the first place, a question that even experts on the [[@mona-lisa|Mona Lisa]] argue about.

The Museum of Broken Relationships started in 2006 as a travelling show by two artists in Croatia, after their own relationship ended. People from many countries sent in objects, such as a toaster, a wedding dress or a garden gnome, each with a short note about what it meant.

The objects themselves are ordinary. The notes make them powerful. It shows how a museum label can change the way you see a thing.

Some museums are famous for their size. The Indian Museum in [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], founded in 1814, is the oldest museum in India. It holds ancient [[sculpture|sculptures]], [[@fossils-form|fossils]], [[@meteorites|meteorites]] and an Egyptian mummy.

[[@smithsonian|The Smithsonian]] in [[@washington-dc|Washington, D.C.]] began with a puzzle. In 1829 James Smithson, an English scientist, died and left his fortune to the United States, a country he had never visited. Gold coins worth over half a million dollars crossed the Atlantic by ship. Congress argued for years, then founded the Smithsonian in 1846. Today it runs about 20 museums and the National Zoo, and most are free to enter.

Many towns have small, unusual museums too: of kites, spoons, typewriters, umbrellas or vintage cars. Some began as one person's hobby that slowly filled a house, then a garage, then a building of its own. Old [[@toys-history|toys]], in particular, fill dozens of museums, because grown-ups love seeing what they once played with. Shankar's International Dolls Museum in Delhi holds thousands of dolls from many countries. A museum does not need a palace. It needs an object, someone who cares about it, and a label that makes you look twice.

text: Cricket commentary began on radio in the 1920s and 1930s. In England, the BBC broadcast its first live cricket descriptions in 1927, only a few decades after [[@radio-invented|radio]] was invented. In India, a Bombay journalist named A. F. S. "Bobby" Talyarkhan gave the first radio commentary in November 1934, from a match at the Bombay Gymkhana. In Australia, broadcasters even faked live coverage of Tests in England, building it in a studio from [[telegraph|telegraph]] messages.

Commentary turned cricket into a shared experience. Before radio, fans had to wait for the next day's newspaper. After it, they could gather around a radio in a shop, a home or a school and follow every ball. They heard about the weather, the crowd and the bowler's run-up as if they were there.

st.prompt: In Australia's 1934 "synthetic" broadcasts, how did listeners hear the sound of the bat hitting the ball?

options.t: A commentator tapped a pencil on a piece of wood
Real recordings were flown from England
A player in the studio hit a ball against the wall

st.reveal: Short telegraph messages arrived from England with the basic facts of each over. Commentators in Sydney turned them into exciting descriptions, adding crowd noise and the "tock" of a pencil on wood as if they were at the ground.

src: BBC, history of Test Match Special.
National Film and Sound Archive of Australia, synthetic cricket broadcasts.

src.Guha R., A Corner of a Foreign Field: The Indian History of a British Sport (Picador, 2002).

d.try: Be a commentator. Watch a few overs of a cricket match, or any sport, with the sound off, and describe it out loud as if you were on the radio. Try to tell your listener the score, who is batting and what the weather is like, without them seeing anything. Then switch roles with a friend.
myth: Radio commentators have always watched the game they describe.

Not in the early days. Australia's synthetic broadcasts in the 1930s were made from short telegraph messages, with commentators far away inventing the details, and sound effects, to make it feel live.

sec.t:
In 1934, Australian fans wanted to follow the Ashes series being played in England. Live radio links across the world were expensive and unreliable. So the Australian Broadcasting Commission tried something clever.

A short [[@telegraph|telegraph]] message, or cable, arrived in Sydney after each over, with the bare facts. Commentators in a studio, who had never seen the play, turned these into lively descriptions. They tapped a pencil on wood for the sound of bat on ball and played recorded crowd noise. Listeners heard what sounded like a live game from the other side of the world. The trick was used again in 1938.

In 1957, the BBC began *Test Match Special*, broadcasting every ball of home [[@test-cricket|Tests]], all five days. Over the years, its commentators became famous for chatting about cakes sent by listeners, pigeons on the pitch and buses passing the ground, filling quiet moments with humour.

One of its best-loved voices, John Arlott, had a slow, rich accent that many fans loved. Commentators learned to paint pictures with words, describing the colour of the sky or the shape of a fielder's shadow, because listeners couldn't see.

In India, radio commentary spread in English, Hindi and other languages. Families crowded around [[transistor|transistor]] radios during big matches, and shopkeepers turned up the volume for passers-by. In the 1980s, colour television and India's 1983 World Cup win made TV commentary hugely popular. Doordarshan broadcast matches to millions of homes across the country.

Today, a big match can have commentary in English, Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Bengali, Marathi and more, broadcast on TV, radio and phones. Some streaming services let viewers pick their language and even their commentator.

A Test match has long gaps: bowlers walking back, drinks breaks and rain. Good commentators fill them with stats, stories and jokes. They need memory, quick thinking and a sense of [[rhythm|rhythm]]. And the best still know when to stay silent and let the roar of the crowd say it all. Some of the stats they quote come from the long and strange story of [[@cricket-records|cricket records]], which commentators know by heart.

text: Virat Kohli is one of the best batters cricket has ever seen. He is famous for chasing big totals in one-day matches, for scoring more one-day international centuries than anyone else, and for his fierce, emotional style. He captained India in all three formats and made the team one of the fittest in the world.

His fame goes beyond cricket. He is one of the most-followed sportspeople anywhere on social media. In India his face sells everything from shoes to insurance, and children copy his celebration after a century.

st.prompt: In the 2023 World Cup semi-final, Kohli hit his 50th one-day international century. Where was the match?

options.t: Wankhede Stadium, Mumbai, with Sachin Tendulkar watching
Eden Gardens, Kolkata
Lord's, London

st.reveal: Kohli broke Sachin's record of 49 ODI hundreds at the Wankhede Stadium, Sachin's home ground, against New Zealand. After reaching 100 he bowed towards Sachin in the stands.

d.try: Try a simple running-between-wickets test. Mark two lines about 17 metres apart, roughly the length of a cricket pitch, and time how long it takes you to run three lengths. Rest, try again, and see if planning your turns makes you faster. Kohli is famous for turning ones into twos.
myth: Kohli was always a super-fit athlete.

Early in his career he has said he ate junk food and was not very fit. Around 2012 he changed his diet and training completely, and he later pushed the whole Indian team to take fitness more seriously.

sec.t:
Kohli was born in [[@delhi|Delhi]] in 1988 and joined the West Delhi Cricket Academy when he was about nine. His coach, Rajkumar Sharma, has said the boy hated losing even in practice.

In December 2006 his father died suddenly in the night. Kohli was 18, and in the middle of a Ranji Trophy match for Delhi against Karnataka. The next morning he went back to bat to save his team, made 90, and only then went to the funeral. Many fans see that day as the moment his determination was set.

Around 2012, Kohli has said, he looked in the mirror and did not like what he saw. He gave up most sweets and fried food, trained in the gym and became much fitter.

As Test captain from 2014 to 2022 he made fitness tests compulsory for the team, including the "yo-yo" running test. India's fast bowlers grew stronger, and India won more Tests under him than under any captain before. In 2018–19 India won its first Test series in Australia.

Kohli's teams often came close but missed out on the big trophies. That changed late in his career. In 2024 he was player of the match in the T20 World Cup final in Barbados, scoring 76, and then retired from T20 internationals. In 2025 India won the Champions Trophy.

He played every [[@ipl|IPL]] season for Royal Challengers Bengaluru, starting in 2008. For years they could not win. In June 2025 they finally beat Punjab Kings in the final in Ahmedabad, and Kohli cried on the field. A month earlier, he had retired from Test cricket.

Kohli shows his feelings openly. He celebrates loudly, argues with opponents and stares down fast bowlers. Some fans love it and say it fires up his team. Critics have said he sometimes goes too far, and he has been fined for on-field behaviour.

Over time he has talked about staying calm and about his [[@mental-health|mental health]]. He has admitted that during a bad tour of England in 2014 he felt lonely even in a room full of people. He is married to the actor Anushka Sharma, and he plays like a man who still hates losing, even at practice.

text: The Antikythera mechanism is a hand-cranked machine made in ancient Greece, probably more than 2,100 years ago. Inside a wooden box about the size of a shoebox were at least 30 interlocking bronze [[@gears|gears]]. Turning a handle moved pointers on dials that showed the positions of the Sun and Moon, the [[@moon-phases|phases of the Moon]], and when [[@eclipses|eclipses]] would happen.

It is often called the world's oldest known analogue computer. Not a computer with a screen, but a machine that calculated by turning one movement into another through gears. It was found in a shipwreck in 1901, and scientists are still working out all its secrets.

st.prompt: Besides eclipses and the Moon, one dial on the Antikythera mechanism tracked a famous event. Which one?

options.t: The four-year cycle of the Olympic Games and other athletic games
The yearly flooding of the Nile
The birthdays of Greek kings

st.reveal: A small dial showed which games, including the Olympics, were due in each year of a four-year cycle. For the Greeks, sport and the sky were both ways of keeping track of time.

src: National Archaeological Museum, Athens, The Antikythera Mechanism.
Freeth T. and others (2006), Decoding the ancient Greek astronomical calculator known as the Antikythera Mechanism. Nature 444.
n.certNote: Scientists agree on what the mechanism did. They still debate exactly when it was made, who built it and whether it also showed all five planets known at the time, because many of its parts are missing.

d.try: Cut two circles from cardboard, one with 10 notches around the edge and one with 20, and pin them so their notches mesh like gears. Turn the small one all the way round once and count how far the big one turns. The Antikythera mechanism used dozens of gear ratios like this to copy the movements of the Sun and Moon.
myth: The Antikythera mechanism is too advanced for its time, so it must be from aliens or time travellers.

It is covered in Greek writing, uses Greek astronomy, and fits with ancient writers such as Cicero, who described similar devices. It shows how skilled Greek craftsmen and astronomers were, not that it came from somewhere else.
facts: 1900–1901, in a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera
probably in the 2nd or early 1st century BCE

sec.t:
For decades the fragments were hard to study. The British scientist Derek de Solla Price spent years on them, and in 1974 published a book, Gears from the Greeks, using early X-ray pictures.

In 2005 a team of scientists brought powerful new X-ray scanners and special cameras to the museum in Athens. The 3D scans showed gears hidden inside the lumps and thousands of tiny Greek letters engraved on the surfaces, a kind of instruction manual. Their results, published in 2006, changed what we knew about the machine.

The front had a big dial showing the [[zodiac|zodiac]] and the 365-day Egyptian calendar. Pointers showed where the Sun and Moon were in the sky. A small ball, half silver and half dark, turned to show the Moon's phase.

The back had two spiral dials. One tracked a 19-year cycle that matches the Moon's months to the solar year. The other predicted [[eclipse|eclipses]] over an 18-year cycle, marking the month and even the hour. Another small dial showed the four-year cycle of athletic games, including the [[@ancient-olympia|Olympics]].

One clever part used a pin and slot between two gears to make the Moon's pointer speed up and slow down. This copied the way the real Moon moves faster at some points in its [[orbit|orbit]]. The [[inscription|inscriptions]] suggest it also showed the five planets visible to the naked eye, though those gears are lost.

Nobody knows. Some researchers link it to [[astronomer|astronomers]] on the island of Rhodes, such as Hipparchus. Others suggest workshops in Corinth or its colonies, perhaps following a tradition going back to [[@ancient-greece|Archimedes]]. The Roman writer Cicero described a bronze sphere made by Archimedes that showed the movements of the Sun, Moon and planets, so similar machines may once have existed. We just haven't found any.

Gear machines this complicated don't appear again in the records for more than a thousand years, until astronomical clocks were built in the Islamic world and in [[medieval|medieval]] Europe. Why the knowledge was lost is a mystery. Perhaps only a few were ever made, and bronze was often melted down and reused.

Today the fragments are displayed at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. Scientists and model makers keep building working copies, each one filling in a few more of the missing gears.

text: A good password is long, hard to guess and used for only one account.

Length matters most. Every extra character multiplies the number of possible passwords a computer would have to try. A string of three or four random, unrelated words, like "lantern purple river tiger", is long and surprisingly easy to remember. Avoid names, birthdays, favourite teams and common words like "password", because guessing programs try those first.

Never reuse the same password everywhere. If one website is hacked, criminals try the stolen password on other sites. And never share your password or a one-time code with anyone except a trusted adult.

st.reveal: The four random words are by far the longest, which multiplies the number of possibilities enormously. "P@ss1!" is short, and "Rahul2014" uses a name and a year, which guessing programs try early. Length and randomness beat clever symbols.

d.try: Take a 3-digit number lock, or draw one on paper. There are 1,000 possible codes, from 000 to 999. Time how long it takes you to try 20 codes. Then work out how long trying all 1,000 would take you. Now think what happens with 4 digits (10,000 codes) and why each extra digit helps so much.
myth: A short password full of symbols, like P@55w0rd, is very strong.

Guessing programs know common swaps like @ for a and 0 for o, and short passwords have fewer possibilities to try. A long password or a string of random words is usually much stronger and easier to remember.
facts: two-step checks, such as a one-time code

sec.t:
Attackers often use computers to try huge numbers of guesses. So the question is: how many possibilities are there?

A 3-digit bicycle lock has 1,000 combinations. A password of 8 lowercase letters has 26 multiplied by itself 8 times, about 200 billion. That sounds like a lot, but a powerful computer can try that many quickly if it has a stolen copy of scrambled passwords. Pick four random words from a list of about 7,000, and the possibilities jump to thousands of trillions, more than 10,000 times as many. You can explore numbers like that in [[@big-numbers|big numbers]].

Passwords are ancient. Roman soldiers used watchwords, passed around the camp each night on a wooden tablet, according to the Greek historian Polybius. A guard would challenge anyone approaching and let them pass only if they knew the word.

Computer passwords began in the early 1960s at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where many people shared one big computer and each needed a private space. Websites don't usually store your actual password. They store a scrambled version made with maths, a relative of the [[@cipher-codes|secret codes]] used for centuries.

Even a strong password can be stolen, for example by a fake website that tricks you into typing it. So many services add a second check. After your password, you might need to enter a one-time code sent to your phone, or approve the login on another device.

In India, one-time codes, or OTPs, protect bank logins and [[@upi-payments|UPI payments]]. Criminals sometimes phone people pretending to be from a bank and ask for the OTP. A real bank will never ask for it.

Most people have dozens of accounts, and nobody can remember dozens of long, different passwords. Password managers help. These apps create strong passwords, store them in an encrypted vault and fill them in for you, so you only need to remember one master password.

Some phones and computers now use passkeys instead, which let you log in with your [[@fingerprint-sensors|fingerprint]], face or a PIN on your own device, without typing a password at all. Whatever you use, the same rule applies, and it's one of the rules in [[@online-safety|staying safe online]]: keep it long, keep it unique, keep it to yourself.

text: नागरिक अधिकार आंदोलन अमेरिका में अश्वेत अमेरिकियों और उनके साथियों का संघर्ष था, ज़्यादातर 1950 और 1960 के दशक में, ताकि क़ानून के नाम पर होने वाला भेदभाव ख़त्म हो।

sec.h: अलग भी, और बराबर भी नहीं
sec.t:
1896 में अमेरिका के [[@supreme-courts|सुप्रीम कोर्ट]] ने [[verdict|फ़ैसला]] दिया कि अलग सुविधाएँ तब तक जायज़ हैं जब तक वे "बराबर" हों। असल में वे लगभग कभी बराबर नहीं होती थीं। अश्वेत बच्चों के स्कूलों की इमारतें अक्सर टूटी-फूटी होतीं और किताबें पुरानी।

एनएएसीपी नाम की एक संस्था के वकील बरसों अदालत में इसके ख़िलाफ़ लड़ते रहे। 1954 में ब्राउन बनाम बोर्ड ऑफ़ एजुकेशन नाम के मुक़दमे में सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने कहा कि स्कूली बच्चों को नस्ल के आधार पर अलग करना [[@us-constitution|संविधान]] के ख़िलाफ़ है। यह मुक़दमा लड़ने वाले वकील थरगुड मार्शल बाद में सुप्रीम कोर्ट के पहले अश्वेत जज बने। दक्षिण के कई राज्यों ने यह आदेश मानने से इनकार कर दिया। 1957 में आर्कंसास के लिटल रॉक में नौ अश्वेत विद्यार्थियों को हाई स्कूल में दाख़िल होने के लिए सैनिकों की हिफ़ाज़त लेनी पड़ी।

1 दिसंबर 1955 को अलाबामा के मॉन्टगोमरी शहर में [[@rosa-parks|रोज़ा पार्क्स]] को गिरफ़्तार कर लिया गया, क्योंकि उन्होंने बस में अपनी सीट एक गोरे आदमी के लिए छोड़ने से इनकार कर दिया था। जवाब में शहर के अश्वेत लोगों ने सिटी बसों में चढ़ना ही बंद कर दिया। वे 381 दिन तक पैदल चले, गाड़ियाँ बाँटकर चलाईं और एक-दूसरे को लाने-ले जाने का इंतज़ाम किया। एक नौजवान पादरी [[@martin-luther-king|मार्टिन लूथर किंग जूनियर]] इस बहिष्कार के नेता बने। 1956 में अदालतों ने वहाँ बसों में अलगाव ख़त्म कर दिया।

28 अगस्त 1963 को "नौकरियों और आज़ादी के लिए वॉशिंगटन मार्च" में लगभग 2.5 लाख लोग वॉशिंगटन डी.सी. में जमा हुए। वहीं किंग ने अपना "आई हैव अ ड्रीम" (मेरा एक सपना है) वाला भाषण दिया।

अगले साल अमेरिकी संसद ने 1964 का नागरिक अधिकार क़ानून पास किया, जिसने सार्वजनिक जगहों पर अलगाव और काम की जगह पर भेदभाव पर रोक लगा दी। 1965 में आंदोलनकारी वोट के हक़ की माँग लेकर अलाबामा के सेल्मा से पैदल निकले। एडमंड पेटस पुल पर पुलिस ने उन पर हमला किया, और इन तस्वीरों ने पूरे देश को झकझोर दिया। कुछ महीनों बाद मतदान अधिकार क़ानून आया, जिसने नाइंसाफ़ी भरी परीक्षाओं के ज़रिए किसी को [[@vote-how|वोट]] डालने से रोकना ग़ैरक़ानूनी बना दिया।

कुछ ही सालों में दक्षिण में अश्वेत मतदाताओं की गिनती तेज़ी से बढ़ी, और अश्वेत अमेरिकी उन पदों पर चुने जाने लगे जिनके दरवाज़े उनके लिए बंद थे। इस आंदोलन से औरतों, लातीनी खेत-मज़दूरों और विकलांग लोगों जैसे दूसरे समूहों को भी बराबरी के हक़ माँगने की हिम्मत मिली।

रातोंरात नाइंसाफ़ी ख़त्म नहीं हुई। स्कूलों, नौकरियों और पुलिस के बर्ताव में बराबरी को लेकर बहस आज भी जारी है। पर देश के क़ानून बदल चुके थे, और यह भी कि ज़्यादातर अमेरिकी [[citizen|नागरिक]] किस बात को ठीक मानते हैं।

text: हम्पी विजयनगर के खंडहर हैं, जो भारत के सबसे महान [[empire|साम्राज्यों]] में से एक की राजधानी थी। लगभग 200 साल तक, 1565 तक, यह दुनिया के सबसे बड़े और सबसे अमीर शहरों में से एक था।

sec.t:
हम्पी की सबसे मशहूर इमारत विट्ठल मंदिर है, जो 15वीं सदी में शुरू हुआ और राजा कृष्णदेवराय के समय में बढ़ाया गया। इसके आँगन में मंदिर-रथ के आकार में तराशा एक छोटा मंदिर खड़ा है, पत्थर के पहियों समेत।

इसे गरुड़ के लिए बनाया गया था, उस गरुड़ के लिए जो भगवान विष्णु का वाहन है। देखने में लगता है कि यह अभी लुढ़क पड़ेगा, पर यह ग्रेनाइट के टुकड़ों से इतनी सफ़ाई से जोड़ा गया है कि जोड़ आसानी से नज़र नहीं आते। दक्षिण भारत में असली मंदिर-रथ लकड़ी के बनते हैं और त्योहारों पर गलियों में खींचे जाते हैं, तो यह रथ पत्थर में उन्हीं की नकल है। यह रथ [[@karnataka|कर्नाटक]] की पहचान बन गया है। 2017 से यह भारत के ₹50 के नोट के पीछे छपता है, यानी करोड़ों लोग अपनी जेब में हम्पी की तस्वीर लेकर घूमते हैं।

विट्ठल मंदिर के मुख्य मंडप में मोटे खंभों के चारों ओर पत्थर के पतले खंभों के झुंड हैं। हल्के से ठोकने पर इनमें से कई साफ़ सुर देते हैं, जैसे पत्थर का कोई विशाल जलतरंग।

आवाज़ हर खंभे के आकार, लंबाई और मोटाई पर निर्भर करती है, ठीक वैसे ही जैसे सितार का छोटा तार लंबे तार से ऊँचा [[@music-notes|सुर]] देता है। बरसों की थपथपाहट से नुक़सान हुआ, इसलिए अब सैलानी इन्हें ठोक नहीं सकते। फिर भी तुम मंडप में खड़े होकर सोच सकते हो कि कभी यहाँ संगीतकार और नर्तक प्रस्तुति देते थे।

हम्पी एक जीता-जागता शहर था। यहाँ हाथियों के अस्तबल हैं, जिनके [[dome|गुंबद]] वाले कमरे शाही हाथियों के लिए काफ़ी बड़े हैं। और है कमल महल, एक सुंदर मंडप जिसके मेहराब पंखुड़ियों जैसे हैं।

सलीके से जोड़े गए हरे पत्थर से बना एक विशाल सीढ़ीदार कुंड कभी अनुष्ठानों के लिए पानी रखता था। पत्थर की नालियाँ शाही इलाके में पानी पहुँचाती थीं। विरूपाक्ष मंदिर, जिसका इतिहास साम्राज्य से भी पुराना है, आज भी पूजा की चहल-पहल वाली जगह है, और इसका ऊँचा गोपुरम पुराने बाज़ार के ऊपर सिर उठाए खड़ा है।

नदी के उस पार आनेगुंदी है, जिसे बहुत से लोग [[@ramayana|रामायण]] के वानर वीरों के राज्य किष्किंधा से जोड़ते हैं। पास की अंजनाद्रि पहाड़ी को बहुत से लोग हनुमान की जन्मभूमि मानते हैं, और [[pilgrimage|तीर्थयात्री]] इसकी 500 से ज़्यादा सीढ़ियाँ चढ़ते हैं।

हम्पी में असली बंदर हर तरफ़ हैं, जो खंडहरों के बीच छलाँगें लगाते और सैलानियों के हाथ से खाना झपटते रहते हैं। 1565 के बाद शहर ज़्यादातर उन्हीं का और किसानों का रह गया। कुछ गाँव वाले आज भी खंडहरों के बीच रहते और खेती करते हैं, और मंदिरों के बीच केले और गन्ना उगाते हैं।

sec.h: शेर आमी और खोई हुई बटालियन
sec.t:
अक्टूबर 1918 में फ़्रांस के आर्गोन जंगल में 500 से ज़्यादा अमेरिकी सैनिक जर्मन फ़ौजों से घिरकर फँस गए। इन्हें "खोई हुई बटालियन" कहा गया। फिर मुसीबत और बढ़ गई: उनकी अपनी ही तोपें ग़लती से उन पर गोले बरसाने लगीं।

उनके कमांडर मेजर चार्ल्स व्हिटलसी ने संदेश बाँधकर कबूतर भेजे। पहले वाले कबूतर मार गिराए गए। आखिरी कबूतर था शेर आमी। उसकी चिट्ठी में मोटे तौर पर लिखा था कि अमेरिकी तोपें अपने ही सैनिकों पर गोले दाग रही हैं, भगवान के लिए इन्हें रोको।

उड़ते ही शेर आमी को गोली लगी। उसकी एक टाँग का बड़ा हिस्सा चला गया, एक आँख ज़ख़्मी हुई और सीने में गोली लगी। फिर भी वह लगभग 25 मिनट में करीब 40 किलोमीटर उड़कर अपने दड़बे तक पहुँच गया। गोलाबारी रुक गई, और लगभग 194 आदमी ज़िंदा बचाए गए।

sec.h: लकड़ी की टाँग और फ़्रांसीसी तमगा

sec.t:
1943 में ब्रिटेन की एक धर्मार्थ संस्था ने युद्ध में बड़ी बहादुरी दिखाने वाले जानवरों के लिए डिकिन मेडल शुरू किया। शुरुआती सालों में यह तमगा किसी भी और जानवर से ज़्यादा कबूतरों को मिला।

पहले पाने वालों में एक थी विंकी। 1942 में एक ब्रिटिश बमवर्षक विमान उत्तरी सागर में गिर गया। चालक दल ने विंकी को छोड़ दिया, और वह तेल से सनी, थकी-हारी, लगभग 190 किलोमीटर उड़कर स्कॉटलैंड में अपने घर पहुँची। उसके पहुँचने के समय से बचाव दल ने मोटा अंदाज़ा लगाया कि जहाज़ कहाँ गिरा होगा, और चालक दल बचा लिया गया।

एक अमेरिकी कबूतर, जी.आई. जो, 1943 में इटली में एक ज़रूरी संदेश लेकर गया। मित्र देशों के विमान एक ऐसे गाँव पर बम गिराने वाले थे जिस पर ब्रिटिश सैनिकों ने अभी-अभी कब्ज़ा किया था। जी.आई. जो का संदेश ठीक समय पर पहुँचा और हमला रोक दिया गया। इससे बहुत-से सैनिकों और गाँव वालों की जान बची।

घर लौटने वाले कबूतर खास तौर पर इसी के लिए पाले जाते हैं कि वे सैकड़ों किलोमीटर दूर से भी अपने दड़बे पर लौट आएँ। वे अक्सर 80 से 100 किलोमीटर प्रति घंटे की रफ़्तार से उड़ते हैं, ज़्यादातर हाईवे पर दौड़ती कार से भी तेज़।

वैज्ञानिकों का मानना है कि वे एक साथ कई सुरागों का इस्तेमाल करते हैं। वे सूरज पर नज़र रखते हैं, [[@earth-magnet|धरती के चुंबकीय क्षेत्र]] को महसूस करते हैं, और घर के पास के निशान पहचानते हैं। कुछ प्रयोगों में कबूतरों पर छोटे-छोटे चुंबक बाँधे गए। बादल वाले दिनों में, जब सूरज नहीं दिखता था, उनमें से कुछ कबूतर रास्ता भटक गए।

लोग हज़ारों सालों से कबूतरों से संदेश भेजते आए हैं। मुग़ल बादशाहों के कबूतरख़ाने थे, और बहुत-से भारतीय राज्यों के भी।

ओडिशा की पुलिस आज भी 100 से ज़्यादा बेल्जियन होमर कबूतर रखती है। पुलिस के मुताबिक कम से कम दो बार ये पक्षी जीवनरेखा बने: 1982 की बाढ़ के बाद और 1999 के महा[[cyclone|चक्रवात]] के बाद, जिसने तट के किनारे-किनारे फ़ोन लाइनें काट दी थीं। आज ये ज़्यादातर स्वतंत्रता दिवस और गणतंत्र दिवस के समारोहों में उड़ते हैं। अब भारत की ज़्यादातर चिट्ठियाँ आधुनिक [[@post-office|डाकघर]] पहुँचाता है, पर पुलिस कहती है कि ओडिशा के कबूतर आने वाली पीढ़ियों के लिए सँभालकर रखे गए हैं।

text: The Galápagos Islands are a group of volcanic islands in the Pacific Ocean, on the [[equator|equator]], about 1,000 kilometres west of Ecuador, the country they belong to. They have never been joined to any continent. Every plant and animal that lives there arrived by flying, swimming, floating or being blown across the sea.

Once they arrived, the newcomers were cut off. Over thousands and millions of years, they changed to suit each island, and many became [[species|species]] found nowhere else. The islands became famous after Charles Darwin visited in 1835, because their animals helped him think about how living things change over time, the idea of [[evolution|evolution]]. Today they are a national park and a living laboratory for scientists.

st.reveal: Peter and Rosemary Grant measured the birds on Daphne Major every year. In the drought, finches with deeper beaks could crack the big, hard seeds that were left, so more of them survived and bred. Their chicks had bigger beaks on average. It was evolution measured in a single generation.

sec.t:
The Galápagos sit above a hotspot, a place where hot rock rises from deep inside the Earth and punches up through the sea floor as volcanoes. The ocean floor slowly slides over the hotspot, carrying older islands away, much like the [[@hawaii-islands|Hawaiian islands]].

The youngest islands, Fernandina and Isabela in the west, are still active. Their black [[lava|lava]] fields look almost bare. The older islands in the east have had time to wear down and grow forests. One recent eruption on Fernandina sent lava flowing into the sea in 2020.

The islands were named after their giant tortoises. In [[@spanish-language|old Spanish]], *galápago* was a word for tortoise. The biggest can weigh over 200 kilograms and live for more than a hundred years. Tortoises on wet, grassy islands have dome-shaped shells. On dry islands, where food grows higher up, some have saddle-shaped shells that let them stretch their necks up to reach cactus pads.

Sailors once took thousands of tortoises onto ships as fresh meat, because they could survive months without food or water. The last tortoise from Pinta Island, nicknamed Lonesome George, died in 2012.

When Darwin visited, he noticed that mockingbirds were different on different islands, and the islanders told him they could tell which island a tortoise came from by its shell. Back in England, an expert told him that his collection of small brown birds were all finches, closely related but with very different beaks.

In 1973, the scientists Peter and Rosemary Grant began measuring finches on the tiny island of Daphne Major, and they kept going for about forty years. After a [[drought|drought]] in 1977, they saw the average beak size grow in a single generation.

The islands' biggest threats today are newcomers. Goats, rats and cats brought by people ate plants, eggs and chicks. Park rangers have removed goats from several islands, one of the largest efforts against [[@invasive-species|invasive species]] ever attempted. Visitors are limited and must stay on marked paths with a trained guide.

text: New Orleans is a port city in Louisiana, near where the [[@mississippi|Mississippi River]] meets the Gulf of Mexico. It was founded by the French in 1718, ruled by Spain for about forty years, then sold to the United States with the [[@usa-statehood|Louisiana Purchase]] in 1803.

Those owners, along with enslaved Africans, free people of colour and later immigrants from Italy, Ireland and the Caribbean, mixed their languages, food and music. The result is a city that sounds, tastes and looks different from anywhere else in America. It is the birthplace of jazz, the home of the biggest Mardi Gras party in the country, and a place that lives with water on every side.
