sec.t:
New Orleans was built on the only firm ground French settlers could find in a swampy bend of the river. As the city grew, swamps were drained and houses spread onto land that slowly sank. Today about half the city lies below sea level, some of it by 2 metres or more.

Tall earth banks called levees hold back the river on one side and a huge lake, Lake Pontchartrain, on the other. Giant pumps push rainwater out. In 2005, when [[@hurricanes|Hurricane Katrina]] struck, several levees failed and about 80 percent of the city flooded. More than a thousand people died in Louisiana, and much of the city had to be rebuilt.

The marshes south of the city used to soften storms before they arrived. They are disappearing as the land sinks and the sea creeps in. The US Geological Survey has estimated that Louisiana loses coastal [[wetland|wetland]] the size of a football field roughly every 100 minutes.

{{story:deltas}}

On Sunday afternoons in the early 1800s, enslaved Africans in New Orleans were allowed to gather in an open space now called Congo Square. They drummed, sang and danced in styles carried from West Africa. Few other American cities allowed this at the time.

Those [[rhythm|rhythms]] mixed with church hymns, military brass bands, [[@blues|the blues]] and the dance music of the Caribbean. By about 1900, musicians were playing something new and loose and full of surprises: [[@jazz|jazz]]. Louis Armstrong was born here in 1901 and grew up playing the cornet. He took the New Orleans sound to Chicago, New York and the whole world.

Mardi Gras means "Fat Tuesday" in French. It is the last day of feasting before Lent, a time when many Christians traditionally give things up. In New Orleans it grows into weeks of parades. Clubs called krewes build giant floats, and riders throw strings of plastic beads to the crowds below.

The official colours are purple, green and gold. Bakeries sell king cake, a ring of sweet dough with a tiny plastic baby hidden inside. Whoever finds the baby in their slice is supposed to bring the cake next time.

sec.h: Gumbo, beignets and two cooking styles
sec.t:
Two cooking traditions meet here. Creole food grew in the city itself, mixing French, Spanish, African and Caribbean cooking. Cajun food came from French-speaking settlers expelled from Canada in the 1700s, who made a new home in the Louisiana swamps.

Both love gumbo, a thick stew of seafood or sausage, often thickened with okra. The word "gumbo" is thought to come from a West African word for okra, the same vegetable Indian kitchens call bhindi. For breakfast, people queue for beignets: square fried doughnuts buried under so much powdered sugar that it snows onto your shirt.

text: British officials and soldiers who lived in Shillong in the 1800s thought it looked like the Scottish Highlands. Its gentle hills are covered in pine forests, with streams, waterfalls and lakes. The weather is cool, misty and often rainy. To homesick Britons, it felt like a little piece of [[@scotland|Scotland]] in the hills of north-east India.

Shillong sits about 1,500 m above sea level, high in the Khasi Hills. It was the capital of British Assam from 1874, and when Meghalaya became a separate state in 1972, it became Meghalaya's capital. Today it's famous for much more than its scenery: for music, football, food, and the culture of the Khasi people.

st.prompt: In many Khasi families in Shillong, which child traditionally inherits the family home?

options.t: The youngest daughter
The eldest son
Whichever child marries first

st.reveal: The Khasi are matrilineal. Children take their mother's clan name, and the youngest daughter, called the khadduh, traditionally inherits the ancestral house and looks after her parents and family traditions.

The name comes from U Shulong, or U Shyllong, a deity the Khasi believe lives on Shillong Peak, the highest point near the city. The Scottish link is only a nickname.

sec.h: A hill station in the clouds
sec.t:
The British built Shillong as a [[@india-wonder-hill-stations|hill station]], a cool place to escape the heat of the plains. They added churches, a golf course and bungalows with sloping tin roofs. Ward's Lake, a small lake with a bridge and gardens, was made in the city centre in the 1890s.

Shillong is only about 50 km from [[@india-wonder-cherrapunji|Cherrapunji]], one of the [[@wettest-place|wettest places]] on Earth. It gets much less rain than that, but still enough to keep its hills green. The Elephant Falls tumble down in three steps just outside the city, and Shillong Peak gives views over the whole valley.

Shillong is often called India's rock music capital. Many homes have a guitar, many churches have [[@choirs|choirs]], and the city is full of [[@indie-music-india|bands]]. Its musicians have played in festivals across India and abroad. Christian missionaries from Wales arrived in the Khasi Hills in the 1840s, and their hymn singing helped give the region its strong love of music.

The best-known is Lou Majaw, who started holding a concert on Bob Dylan's birthday, 24 May, in 1972, and kept doing it for decades. Western [[@rock-music|rock]], [[@blues|blues]] and country songs have been popular here since the 1960s, and many young Khasi musicians now write songs in their own language too.

Shillong has an unusual daily game called teer. Members of archery clubs shoot hundreds of arrows at a straw target in a field. The number of arrows that hit is counted, and people bet on the last two digits of that number. It is a legal, licensed lottery, and results are posted every afternoon.

Football is the other big sport. Local clubs have produced players for India's national team, and big matches fill the stadium with noise. After the game, people head for jadoh, a Khasi dish of rice cooked with pork, or tungrymbai, made from fermented soybeans. In autumn, cherry trees bloom pink across the hills, and Shillong holds a cherry blossom festival, adding one more surprise to a city that already feels a long way from the plains.

text: Nobody planned the order for English. We inherited it, almost letter by letter, from a chain of older alphabets: Latin from Rome, Greek before that, and before the Greeks, the [[@phoenicians|Phoenicians]] and their neighbours in the eastern Mediterranean.

Clay tablets from the ancient city of Ugarit, in today's Syria, list letters in nearly the same sequence about 3,400 years ago. Their list began aleph, beth, gimel, daleth, which became our A, B, C, D. Why those early writers lined them up that way is a genuine mystery. Some scholars think it helped children memorise them, maybe as a chant. Others think the order is simply an accident that stuck.

st.prompt: The Hindi varnamala starts a, aa, i, ii and then ka, kha, ga, gha. Why that order?

options.t: Sounds are grouped by where in your mouth you make them, from throat to lips
The most common letters come first
It copies the order of the English alphabet

st.reveal: Ancient Indian grammarians grouped sounds scientifically. The ka row is made at the back of the throat, and each row moves forward until the pa row on the lips. Say them slowly and feel your tongue travel.

n.certNote: The history of the order is well traced back to about 1400 BCE. Why the first letter-makers picked that order in the first place is unknown, and scholars have only guesses.

sec.t:
The early Latin alphabet had Z in seventh place, where Greek had zeta. Around 300 BCE the Romans decided they didn't need it, because the sound had vanished from Latin, and dropped it.

That left a gap. Romans had been using C for both the "k" and "g" sounds, which caused confusion. So they made a new letter by adding a little bar to C, creating G, and slotted it into Z's old seat. Two centuries later, when educated Romans wanted to write Greek words, they brought Z back. Its old place was taken, so it went to the end of the line, along with Y.

For centuries, I and J were the same letter, and so were U and V. Printers in the 1500s and 1600s slowly started treating them as separate letters. W began as two Vs or two Us written together, which is why we still call it "double U". In French it is "double V".

English children in the 1800s even recited "&" after Z as if it were a letter. They ended with "and per se and", which slurred over time into the word "ampersand".

There was once a rival alphabet order, beginning h, l, ḥ, m. It was used in ancient South Arabia, and it survives today in Ethiopia. Ethiopia's Ge'ez script, used for Amharic, still starts with ha, la, ḥa, ma. A child in Addis Ababa learns a completely different sequence from a child in Chicago, both descended from the same early experiments.

Indian scripts took a very different path. Over 2,000 years ago, Sanskrit grammarians studied exactly how the mouth makes each sound, and arranged the alphabet to match. Vowels come first. Then consonants march from the throat (ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa) to the palate, the roof of the mouth, the teeth and finally the lips (pa, pha, ba, bha, ma).

Each row follows the same pattern of plain, breathy, voiced, breathy-voiced and nasal sounds. Devanagari, Bengali, Tamil, Kannada and other [[@scripts-india|Indian scripts]] all use versions of this order. It is one of the most logical alphabets ever arranged, built by the careful thinkers behind [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]].

Looking up a word in an English dictionary means following a sequence that is about 3,400 years old. Putting words in that order was a later invention, and the people who first tried it have a story of their own in [[@dictionaries|dictionaries]].

text: Milk turns into curd because of [[bacteria|bacteria]]. You warm some [[@milk|milk]], let it cool until it feels just warm on your finger, and stir in a spoonful of curd from yesterday. That spoonful contains huge numbers of lactic [[acid|acid]] bacteria.

Over the next few hours, the bacteria feed on [[lactose|lactose]], the natural sugar in milk, and turn it into lactic acid. The acid makes the milk [[protein|proteins]] unravel and link up into a soft, wobbly gel that traps the water. By morning the liquid milk has become thick, tangy curd. The sour taste is the acid. The thickness is the protein net.

st.reveal: The bacteria that make curd work best when they're warm, a bit warmer than your skin. In the cold they slow right down. A warm, covered spot helps them grow, and the curd sets in hours instead of a whole day.

myth: All curd and yogurt contains living bacteria.
Fresh homemade curd does. But some shop yogurts are heated after they set, which kills the bacteria. Labels that say "live cultures" mean the bacteria are still alive.

sec.t:
In Indian homes, the spoonful of old curd is called the starter or *jaamun*. It carries a whole community of [[microbe|microbes]]. Families pass starters to neighbours, and a new bride sometimes brings one from her mother's kitchen.

Because each starter has its own mix of microbes, curd can taste a little different from house to house. Scientists who study traditional Indian curd find many kinds of lactic acid bacteria in it, along with some [[yeast|yeasts]]. Commercial yogurt is usually made with just two carefully chosen bacteria.

The bacteria in curd grow best between about 30 and 45°C. That is why curd sets quickly in May and slowly in December. If the milk is too hot, the bacteria die. If it is too cold, they hardly move.

So families keep curd somewhere snug in winter, wrapped in a cloth or tucked inside a closed casserole. In the past, some kept clay pots of curd near the warm kitchen fire. Clay also soaks up some water, which helps make the curd extra thick, as in Bengal's famous sweet *[[@bengali-food|mishti doi]]*.

Curd cools a meal in hot weather and calms a fiery curry. It becomes raita with cucumber, [[@lassi-chaas|chaas]] or lassi when whisked with water, and kadhi when cooked with gram flour. In Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, a meal often ends with curd rice.

In India, "curd" means dahi. In Britain and America, "curds" usually means the lumps that form when making cheese, so Indian visitors abroad sometimes find the word confusing.

The acid in curd keeps many harmful germs from growing, which is why it was a safe way to store milk before [[@refrigerator|fridges]]. Some of its lactose has already been used up by bacteria, so many people who get tummy aches from milk can eat curd.

Live bacteria in curd may also join the [[@microbes-friendly|friendly microbes]] in your [[@digestion-gut|gut]] for a while. Researchers are studying how much they help. What is clear is that a bowl of curd is a good source of protein and calcium, and it has been part of Indian meals for thousands of years.

text: Most of the world eats grains every day. A grain is the dry seed of a grass plant, packed with [[starch|starch]]. Three grains matter most: maize (corn), wheat and rice. According to the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization, these three provide around half of the food energy people eat around the world.

Other grains matter a lot too. Barley, sorghum, oats and millets feed hundreds of millions of people, especially in dry places. In India, a plate might hold rice in Kolkata, wheat rotis in Lucknow and ragi balls in rural Karnataka. Across the world, grain is cheap, keeps for months and fills you up. That is why so many great [[civilisation|civilisations]] were built on it.

st.prompt: Which of these is NOT really a grain from a grass?

options.t: Quinoa
Ragi (finger millet)
Barley

st.reveal: True grains are the seeds of grasses. Ragi and barley are grasses, but quinoa comes from a leafy plant related to spinach. People cook it like a grain, so it is often called a pseudo-grain.

sec.t:
[[@rice|Rice]] was first farmed along the Yangtze River in China, about 9,000 years ago. It grows best in warm, wet fields, often flooded with water. Today about nine out of every ten bowls of rice are grown and eaten in Asia.

India became the world's largest rice grower in 2024–25, with about 150 million tonnes, just ahead of China. India is also the biggest rice exporter, sending basmati and other rice to the Middle East, Africa and beyond. In the United States, rice grows mostly in Arkansas, California and Louisiana.

Maize began as a wild grass called teosinte in what is now Mexico, around 9,000 years ago. Its ears were tiny, about the size of your little finger. Over thousands of years, farmers picked seeds from the best plants, until it became the big cob we know.

Today maize is the most-grown grain on Earth, at well over a billion tonnes a year. The United States grows the most, mainly in the Corn Belt of Iowa, Illinois and nearby states. But most maize is fed to cows, pigs and chickens, or made into ethanol fuel, corn syrup and starch. Only a part of it ends up as tortillas, cornflakes or bhutta roasted on a street corner.

Before rice and wheat spread across India, many families ate [[@millets|millets]] such as jowar (sorghum), bajra (pearl millet) and ragi (finger millet). Millets grow with little water and handle heat well. India is the world's biggest millet grower.

The UN named 2023 the International Year of Millets, after a proposal from India. Millets are now showing up again in school meals, breakfast cereals and city cafes. As the [[climate|climate]] warms, crops that cope with [[drought|drought]] may become more important.

There are thousands of edible plants, so it is odd that we lean so heavily on a handful. Grains are easy to store, carry and trade, and they produce a lot of food per field. But depending on a few crops is risky. One disease or drought can hurt harvests in many countries at once.

That is why scientists keep seeds of thousands of grain varieties in seed banks, including a vault dug into a frozen mountain in Svalbard, Norway. If a crop fails, an old variety stored there might hold the answer.
